opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that if you separate research from product, you end up optimizing for the wrong things. A lot of research labs build very capable models against benchmarks and then hand them off to a product team who tries to figure out what to do with them. The problem is that benchmarks are a proxy, and often a pretty poor one, for what actually matters when a real person is trying to get real work done.

Our view at Reflection is that the path to superintelligence runs through autonomous agents, systems that can actually do meaningful work on their own over long horizons. And we think the most natural place to start is coding, because so much of what an agent needs to do eventually gets expressed through code. But if you want to build a truly capable coding agent, you have to be close to the problems engineers actually face. That's not "write a function that passes a unit test." It's "understand this enormous, messy codebase that's been evolving for ten years, figure out why this thing broke, and fix it without breaking three other things." You only learn what those problems really look like by putting a product in front of customers and watching where it fails.

So the product becomes the source of truth for the research. It tells you what capabilities are missing, it generates the right kind of signal and data, and it keeps you honest. And in the other direction, the research shapes what the product can be. You're not just wrapping someone else's model and making UX decisions around its limitations. You can actually go change the model when you find a gap.

Misha and I both came from places like DeepMind, where we saw how powerful it is when you have a tight loop between the system and the environment it's learning from. AlphaGo didn't get superhuman by being evaluated on a static test set. It got there by having a really rich environment and a clear reward signal. Product, in a sense, is that environment for us. Co-designing the two is how you get that tight feedback loop in the real world rather than in a game.

So for us it's not a business decision layered on top of research. It's actually the research strategy. We think it's the fastest way to get to systems that are genuinely superhuman at useful work.

r002.rationale: It describes learning from a customer-facing product, but does not propose working backward from how superintelligence will be deployed in users’ hands.

r003.rationale: It says the product is the source of truth for research and reveals which capabilities are missing, directly linking product needs to capabilities researchers develop.

r004.rationale: It presents coding agents as a starting point and autonomous agents as the path to superintelligence, but does not argue that co-design is preferable because the product category is broad enough to elicit superintelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it comes out of a lesson we learned the hard way at DeepMind. When I was there, working on Gemini and before that on reinforcement learning, we had this incredible research culture, but research and product lived in very different worlds. You'd build something in the lab, it would work beautifully on a benchmark, and then the moment it touched a real workflow, you'd discover the benchmark was measuring the wrong thing. The failure modes that actually matter, the long-horizon ones, the ones where an agent has to recover from a mistake it made twenty steps ago, those don't show up unless the system is actually doing real work for someone.

So when Ioannis and I started Reflection, the core bet was that the path to superintelligence runs through autonomous agents that do economically meaningful work, and you can't make those agents good in the abstract. You need a tight loop. The product tells you where the model breaks. The research fixes it. The fixed model unlocks a harder task in the product, and you go around again. That's why we started with coding. It's a domain where the feedback is dense, where correctness is verifiable, and where the agent has to plan over long horizons. It's basically the ideal environment for reinforcement learning, but with the reward signal coming from reality instead of from a contrived task we designed.

The other piece is that I think a lot of people treat product as a distraction from the research mission, like it's the thing you do to pay the bills. I see it the opposite way. If you look at what made AlphaGo work, it wasn't just the algorithms, it was that Go gave you a perfectly specified environment with unlimited self-play. The hard part of building general agents is that the real world doesn't hand you that environment. You have to build it. And the product is the environment. Every user interaction, every task that succeeds or fails, that's the data that teaches the model what competence actually looks like.

So co-design isn't a compromise for us. It's the methodology. The research people need to feel the pain of the product breaking, and the product people need to understand what the model can and can't learn from. If those two groups are separated, you end up optimizing for things that look impressive in a demo and fall apart under real use.

r001.rationale: The response discusses building agents and learning from real work, but does not say superintelligence has already been achieved in narrow domains.

r002.rationale: It describes a product–research feedback loop and a path through economically meaningful work, but does not clearly propose working backward from how superintelligence will be deployed in users’ hands.

r003.rationale: It says the product reveals where the model breaks and that the research fixes those failures, with coding tasks shaping the capabilities developed, such as planning over long horizons.

r004.rationale: It calls coding an ideal environment for reinforcement learning, but does not argue that the product category is broad enough to elicit superintelligence.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that product and research should form a feedback loop. Research gives you new capabilities, but putting those capabilities into a product tells you whether they actually work on the problems people care about. It exposes things that are very easy to miss when you’re just looking at benchmarks.

That’s especially important for agents. A model can give a very impressive answer in one interaction, but can it carry out a task over many steps, recognize when something went wrong, and recover? When you build the product alongside the research, those failures become concrete research questions. And when you solve them, you can immediately see whether you’ve made the system more useful.

So I don’t think of product as something you attach after the research is done. It’s part of how you figure out what to research. The goal is to have the work that makes the product better also move you toward more general, more capable intelligence.

r003.rationale: It says product use exposes failures that become concrete research questions and that product helps determine what to research.

r004.rationale: It does not argue that the product category should be broad enough to elicit superintelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
The reason is that I think product and research should form a feedback loop. Research gives you new capabilities, but putting those capabilities into a product tells you whether they actually work on problems people care about. And the failures you see in real use can point you toward the next research problem.

That’s especially important when you’re building agents. A model can look very strong on a benchmark and still struggle to complete a useful task end to end. When you build the product alongside the model, you’re forced to confront that gap: Can it work reliably? Can it recover from mistakes? Can it tell when it needs more information?

So for us, the product is also a way to ground the research. You want the research to expand what’s possible, and you want real use to keep you honest about how far you’ve actually gotten. Co-designing them makes that loop much tighter.
